notes.purpose: Problem, solution, proof and the ask in one view.
notes.script: Problem: the median loan funds in 2.85 days, but a quarter wait more than 15.95 days, and same-day funding fell from 46.0 to 30.3 percent. Solution: loan details predict which loans will be slow, so Kiva can send lender-side support there first: a boosted tree on loan structure catches the slowest fifth 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance. Proof: rewriting stories is not the lever, because five framings stay within five percent of funding time. Our ask: pilot the flag with lender-side support, and test one truthful prompt before giving writing advice. For whom and when is still open: no reliable difference so far, with subgroup results pending.

slides.decision: Our ask to Kiva: pilot a slow-funding flag with lender-side support, and test one truthful prompt.
slides.pending: For whom and when: no period, loan size, gender or region shows a large framing effect; a few rare-word patterns are hypotheses to test.

slides.title: Borrowers usually have the money before lenders fund the loan
slides.subtitle: Descriptive: how a typical pre-disbursed Kiva loan moves, who acts at each stage, and what we measure

body.text: 1,453,846 input records; 6 negative durations excluded; 1,637 refunded records included.

takeaways.heading: We study the lender-side step
takeaways.text: Our outcome runs from **listing to full funding**, median 2.85 days.

takeaways.heading: Borrowers usually already have the money
takeaways.text: **96.4% of loans** reach the borrower a median **24.2 days** before listing.

takeaways.heading: Speed turns over partner capital
takeaways.text: Only **3.6%** are paid out after listing, so slow funding mainly holds up the partner’s next loans.

takeaways.heading: Unfunded loans are missing
takeaways.text: Only loans that **eventually funded** are in the data; expired listings are not.

notes.purpose: How a Kiva loan works, and which step we measure.
notes.script: Five stages and four actors. The field partner usually pays the borrower first; Kiva then reviews and lists the loan; lenders fund it; Kiva passes the funds to the partner; and the borrower repays the partner, which repays lenders. For 96.4 percent of loans the borrower already had the money, a median 24.2 days before listing. So the time we measure, from listing to full funding, median 2.85 days, is a lender-side delay: it decides how fast the partner's capital is replenished. Only loans that eventually funded are in the data, so expired listings are missing.
notes.reference: docs/1_data_dictionary.md (disbursalDate); funding duration in the claims register.

notes.purpose: Define the problem in lender-time terms.
notes.script: Two views of the wait. The yearly chart: same-day funding fell from 42.5 percent in 2019 to 32.3 percent in 2020, a fall of 10.2 points in one year, and stayed near 28 to 30 percent. At the same time the share of loans waiting more than two weeks rose from 19.2 to 35.8 percent; in 2021 that was 55,408 loans. The median wait rose from 1.72 days in 2019 to 4.57 days in 2020 and stayed between 4.49 and 5.35 days through 2024. 2025 may be incomplete, because loans still unfunded at extraction are missing. The strip shows all years together: the median loan is funded in 2.85 days and a quarter within 0.39 days, but a quarter wait more than 15.95 days. That long, predictable tail is why an early-warning flag matters.

notes.purpose: Where the loans and the delays are.
notes.script: Where the loans sit, and where they wait. Ten of 48 countries hold 81 percent of loans, and Asia and Africa 92.8 percent. Speed varies widely: same-day funding runs from 15 percent in Pakistan to 67 percent in Madagascar, and the median wait from 1.13 days in the Philippines to 14.0 days in Tajikistan. In all, 393,847 loans, 27.1 percent, waited more than two weeks, and three countries, Kenya, the Philippines and Tajikistan, hold 56.1 percent of them. Long waits are not a small-country problem: 36.4 percent of Kenya's loans and half of Tajikistan's wait over two weeks. That is why the early warning has to be validated country by country: its precision ranges from 0.18 to 0.90 across the largest countries.
notes.reference: reports/evidence_sources/country_shares.json (src/country_shares.py); map: scripts/build_country_map.py.

slides.title: Slow funding is a lender-side delay that loan details predict, not wording
slides.subtitle: Three findings across the outcome audit, the early-warning check and the equivalence test, each leading to a step of the solution

cards.heading: The wait is on the lender side
cards.text: of loans reach the borrower before listing

cards.heading: Loan details predict who waits
cards.text: better than chance at flagging the slowest fifth

cards.heading: Wording makes little difference
cards.text: five framings stay within this share of funding time

notes.purpose: Bridge from the problem to the evidence and the solution.
notes.script: Three findings point the same way, and each leads to a step of the solution. First, the wait is on the lender side: 96.4 percent of loans reach the borrower before listing, a median 24.2 days earlier, so the lever is helping slow loans find lenders. Second, loan details predict who waits: a boosted tree on structure flags the slowest fifth 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance. Third, wording makes little difference: five framings stay within five percent of funding time, and text adds little to the flag. That holds across every period, loan size, gender and region we checked, while a few rare-word patterns remain hypotheses to test. So the lever is helping slow loans find lenders, not rewriting their stories. The next slides show the evidence behind each insight.
notes.reference: docs/1_data_dictionary.md (disbursalDate); reports/evidence_sources/triage_summary.json; equivalence screen; reports/evidence_sources/robustness_summary.json.

notes.purpose: Explain how the evidence fits together.
notes.script: All four analyses use the same loans, and each feeds a part of the solution. The explanatory models ask which features are linked to speed, using regressions of funding time and same-day funding with errors clustered by country; because these are associations, they feed the Test step. The robustness checks rerun them with more text measures and a programme proxy, and the equivalence test asks which links are small enough to bound. Together they feed Prioritise: do not chase framing tweaks. The forecast benchmark trains on earlier years and tests each year with and without text; with the early-warning check it feeds Predict. Its numbers are not comparable with the others. Four add-on checks strengthen this: a wild cluster bootstrap and subgroup refits test whether the small associations hold, the gain by feature group shows where the forecast gain comes from, and the early-warning check tests whether a forecast can flag slow loans. The strip shows the years: the explanatory work uses all loans, the holdout tests on 2024 and 2025, and the benchmark retrains five times, each only on loans completed before the test year. None of these is a causal claim.

slides.title: Clustering by country removed 64 of 120 significant terms
slides.subtitle: Explanatory models: HC3 versus 48-country clustered errors on 1,453,840 loans

takeaways.heading: Few countries dominate
takeaways.text: Ten countries hold **81% of loans**; regional patterns rest on **two countries each**.

takeaways.heading: Text terms are hit hardest
takeaways.text: **42 of 56 text terms** lost significance, against 22 of 64 controls.

takeaways.heading: Few text terms survive
takeaways.text: Only **14** stay significant: sentiment in both models and 12 family-framing interactions.

takeaways.heading: Urgency no longer passes
takeaways.text: Its p-value rose from below 0.001 to **0.49** for funding time and 0.22 for same-day funding.

notes.purpose: Show why we distrust headline significance.
notes.script: With 1.45 million rows almost everything looks significant, because standard HC3 errors treat every loan as independent. When we let errors correlate within each of 48 countries, 64 of the 120 significant terms fell away. [Point: Few countries dominate] The reason is concentration: ten countries hold 81 percent of loans and behave very differently, and regional family-framing patterns rest on two countries each, so they support no regional writing rules; the appendix shows the check. [Point: Text terms are hit hardest] Most of the terms lost are text terms. [Point: Few text terms survive] Only sentiment and some family interactions remain, and the next slide tests the framing terms harder. [Point: Urgency no longer passes] Urgency is the clearest case. For the solution, this means three things: report country-clustered uncertainty rather than only loan-level errors, validate the slow-funding flag country by country before using it, and give no country or regional writing rules from two-country regions. Losing significance is weak evidence, not evidence of no effect; the next two slides ask what survives programme controls and how small the remaining links are.

notes.purpose: Show that not everything disappears.
notes.script: Under richer programme controls, only two terms looked like signals: third-person framing for funding time and business framing for same-day funding. With 48 countries, the usual clustered test can be too generous, so we re-ran every term with a wild cluster bootstrap, 9,999 draws with Webb weights. After adjusting for nine terms, the lowest p-value is 0.136, so neither survives. What remains is tiny: business framing is linked to about a quarter of a percentage point in same-day funding per extra mention. [Point: Pronouns may reflect the writer] Descriptions are usually written by partner staff, so the third-person link may say more about who writes than about the borrower. The next slide asks how small the remaining links really are.

notes.purpose: Separate 'small' from 'unknown'.
notes.script: Answer first: five of the nine framings have small links to funding time; urgency and first person remain unknown. How to read the chart: each dot is the estimated change in funding time per extra mention per 100 words, and its line is the 90 percent range. Left of the centre line means faster funding, right means slower. The darker yellow area is within plus or minus five percent of funding time, which we treat as too small to matter; the lighter area runs from five to ten percent. A line that sits wholly inside the darker area means the link is small. [Point: Five framings have small links] Family, business, basic needs, agency and third person sit inside it in both model versions: the expanded model shown here and the programme-adjusted model. Gratitude and sentiment are small only in the programme-adjusted model. [Point: Small means under five hours] Five percent sounds abstract: on a typical loan, which takes 2.85 days to fund, it is about four and a half to four point seven hours. [Point: Urgency is too rare to judge] Urgency and first person appear in under two percent of descriptions, as the right-hand bars show, so their ranges stay wide: up to six to fourteen percent faster or slower. That is not evidence of an effect, or of none. [Point: The verdicts hold under stricter tests] Technically, the band is plus or minus 0.05 on log of one plus days, tested with two one-sided tests, BH-adjusted across nine terms, using a t reference with 47 degrees of freedom. With a stricter t(4) reference all five verdicts hold, and family, agency and third person stay small even at plus or minus two percent. We set the band after seeing the estimates, so this is exploratory. A wild cluster bootstrap across 48 countries, with 9,999 draws, confirms the screen: 35 of 36 verdicts are unchanged and 22 of 23 bounded results survive; the one loss is basic needs for same-day funding in the programme-adjusted model.

notes.purpose: Answer for whom and when.
notes.script: For whom and when: we refitted the programme-adjusted model separately in ten subgroups: three periods, three loan sizes, female and male borrowers, and Asia and Africa, and applied the same five percent equivalence test. Family, business, agency, third person, basic needs and gratitude stay small in all ten; sentiment in nine. So the small result is not an average hiding a large effect in one group, and no period or loan-size interaction survives country clustering. Rare words stay unresolved: urgency is small in one subgroup, first person in five. Among about 180 unadjusted tests, urgency in Asia and agency by gender stand out; they are hypotheses for the Test step, not findings. For same-day funding the pattern is weaker: business and third person are small in all ten, family and agency in nine. In the expanded model, family, business, agency and third person stay small in all ten. The bounds were set after the estimates, so this is exploratory.

notes.purpose: Keep text in proportion: it helps forecasts a little and does not drive triage.
notes.script: Text does carry forecast information: added to loan structure it lowered error in every test year, by 0.26 to 0.39 days, about seven hours at the median. Most of that comes from word patterns; the lexicon and sentiment measures closest to framing add 0.003 to 0.055 days. On its own, text forecasts worse than loan structure alone, by 0.146 to 1.032 days, and adding it barely changes the slow-funding flag. That is why the flag is built on loan details. The next slide shows how fragile the gain is across countries.

takeaways.heading: Text helps in every year
takeaways.text: Month-resampled ranges stay **above zero in 5 of 5 years**; the median gain is about **7 hours**.

takeaways.heading: The gain needs word patterns
takeaways.text: The tree model, without TF-IDF, gains **at most 0.04 days**.

takeaways.heading: Across countries it is fragile
takeaways.text: Country resampling **includes zero in 4 of 5 years**; capping extreme forecasts leaves zero in **1 of 5**.

notes.purpose: Keep the gain in proportion.
notes.script: Answer first: the text gain holds every year, but it is fragile across countries. Three panels, read in order. [Point: Text helps in every year] Panel a resamples calendar months: all five ranges sit right of zero, and the median gain is 0.293 days, about seven hours. [Point: The gain needs word patterns] Panel b sets the linear model, which uses TF-IDF word patterns, against the tree model, which has form and lexicon but no TF-IDF: the tree gains at most 0.04 days. [Point: Across countries it is fragile] Panel c resamples countries instead: four of five ranges include zero. Capping forecasts at the longest training wait, 173.4 days, a diagnostic rather than the reported model, leaves only 2025 including zero, so much of the fragility comes from a few extreme forecasts. Metrics also disagree at the margin: in 2025 text improved error and calibration, but AUC for same-day funding fell from 0.893 to 0.888. Each range uses 1,000 resamples; these are fixed-model resampling ranges, not retraining or causal uncertainty.

notes.purpose: Turn the evidence into a framework Kiva can act on.
notes.script: Three steps. Predict: at posting time, score each listing’s risk of slow funding. In a retrospective check on the November benchmark, a boosted tree using loan structure flags the slowest fifth of loans 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance; adding text barely changes it. Prioritise: send lender-side support, such as featuring, matching funds, lender alerts and partner follow-up, to the flagged loans, and do not chase framing tweaks, because framing links stay within five percent of funding time. Test: before any writing advice, pass three gates: validate the measures, close the data gaps, and pilot one truthful clarity prompt against a control. Later, a data partnership with listing-time text and unfunded listings would let us answer for whom and when properly. If a gate fails, stop there and report the uncertainty.

notes.purpose: Show what acting on the evidence could look like, without overclaiming.
notes.script: This is a concept to pilot, not a product. When a loan is posted, a model scores its risk of slow funding from its structure: amount, term, sector, country and timing. Flagged loans get lender-side support. In a retrospective check on 2021 to 2025, flagging the top ten percent of predicted-slow loans caught the slowest fifth 2.6 to 4.0 times better than chance with a boosted tree; adding text barely changed it. Results are uneven across countries, the check only covers loans that eventually funded, and the predicted probabilities drift in 2025, so they need recalibrating before use as thresholds. A flag says a loan is likely slow, not why.

slides.subtitle: Proposed levers for Kiva and partners; their effect on speed is to be tested, not yet measured

levers.name: Feature it
levers.text: Show flagged loans to lenders early on the lending page.

levers.name: Match it
levers.text: Offer matching funds where a loan is likely to stall.

levers.name: Alert lenders
levers.text: Notify lenders who follow the loan’s sector or country.

levers.name: Follow up
levers.text: Ask the field partner to check the listing is complete and clear.

dont.text: Five framings stay within ±5% of funding time, about 4.5–4.7 hours on a typical loan, and text adds little to the flag.

slides.note: Scope: the levers are proposals; our data do not measure their effect, so each needs a controlled pilot.

notes.purpose: What to do with a flag.
notes.script: A flag only helps if something happens next. We propose four lender-side levers: feature flagged loans early, offer matching funds where a loan is likely to stall, alert lenders who follow the sector or country, and ask the partner to check the listing is complete. Our data do not measure what these levers do, so each needs a pilot. What we can say is where not to spend effort: framing tweaks, because five framings stay within five percent of funding time, about four and a half hours on a typical loan.

notes.script: Before anyone tells borrowers how to write, three things need to happen, in order. First, check that our word counts measure what we think. Second, get the data we are missing: what lenders saw and the listings that never funded. Third, test one truthful prompt with partners. [Point: Each gate unlocks a stronger claim] Each gate lets us say a little more, from associations today to a tested effect of editing. If a gate fails, we stop and report the uncertainty.

slides.title: Four guardrails keep the solution honest
slides.subtitle: What this evidence cannot show, and what to do about it

notes.purpose: Limits, each with an action.
notes.script: Four guardrails. One: every result is an association; nothing has been tested by editing a description or applying a lever, so each needs a controlled pilot. Two: only funded loans are in the data, so we cannot say whether a lever helps loans that would otherwise expire. Three: the flag is uneven across countries, with precision from 0.18 to 0.90 within the ten largest, and its probabilities drift in 2025, so it must be recalibrated and validated by country. Four: for whom and when is still open; regional patterns rest on two countries each, and subgroup results are pending. Funding time is also a platform measure: 96.4 percent of loans reach the borrower before listing.
notes.reference: claims register; reports/evidence_sources/triage_summary.json; appendix A6.

blocks.question: Associations, not causes
blocks.evidence: Every result is observational; no edit or lever has been tested.
blocks.so_what: Pilot each lever and prompt against a control.

blocks.question: Funded loans only
blocks.evidence: Listings that expired unfunded are not in the data, so reach is unknown.
blocks.so_what: Add expired listings before judging reach.

blocks.question: Uneven across countries
blocks.evidence: Flag precision within the 10 largest countries; probabilities drift in 2025.
blocks.so_what: Recalibrate and validate the flag country by country.

blocks.question: For whom and when
blocks.evidence: Six framings stay small in every period, loan size, gender and region; rare words stay open.
blocks.so_what: Test urgency in Asia as a hypothesis.

notes.purpose: Backup: why the regional family-framing patterns support no regional advice.
notes.script: Answer first: the two regional family-framing links look strong, but each rests on two countries. How to read it: each panel is one region; the dot is the average change in funding time per extra family mention per 100 words, and the lines are 95 percent ranges. Left of the centre line is faster funding. [Point: Both links look strong at first] With standard country-clustered errors the ranges sit well left of zero: minus 0.1003 to minus 0.0456 in the Middle East and minus 0.0879 to minus 0.0605 in Central America, about seven percent faster per mention. [Point: Two countries cannot carry them] With only two countries, between-country uncertainty cannot be estimated well. A t(1) reference on the same clustered error, a heuristic screen rather than a calibrated test, widens the ranges to minus 0.2502 to plus 0.1043 and minus 0.1629 to plus 0.0145; heuristic p-values are 0.1203 and 0.0597. The bars show the country mix: the Middle East is 97 percent Palestine, so it is close to a one-country result. [Point: Other regions have many more countries] Africa has 27 countries and Asia 12, which is why only these two thin regions are singled out here. [Point: No regional writing rules yet] These are descriptive patterns, not grounds for country or regional writing rules; a real test needs more countries per region or partner-level data.

slides.title: Adding text lowered forecast error in 5 of 5 years
slides.subtitle: Forecast benchmark: linear model, structure only versus structure plus text, identical evaluation rows

exhibit.caption: Linear-model MAE in days (top) and its reduction by text feature group (bottom), identical evaluation rows.
exhibit.note_sup: Groups added in order: form, then lexicon and sentiment, then TF-IDF; another order would split the gain differently.

takeaways.heading: Text carries forecast information
takeaways.text: Gains of **0.26–0.39 days** on 728,640 evaluation records.

takeaways.heading: Forecasting is not persuasion
takeaways.text: Text may encode **purpose, place or programme templates**, not only persuasion.

takeaways.heading: No single country drives it
takeaways.text: Removing any single country **leaves the gain positive** in every year (exploratory check).

takeaways.heading: Word patterns carry most of it
takeaways.text: TF-IDF gives the largest share in **4 of 5 years**; lexicon and sentiment add only **0.003–0.055 days**.

notes.purpose: Present the strongest new result.
notes.script: We trained on earlier years and tested on each of 2021 to 2025, comparing the same model with and without text on the same loans. Text reduced error every year. [Point: Word patterns carry most of it] Splitting the gain by feature group, added in a fixed order, word patterns from TF-IDF give most of it in four of five years; 2023 is the exception, where description form leads. The lexicon, specificity and sentiment measures, the ones closest to framing, add only 0.003 to 0.055 days. Text alone forecasts worse than structure alone in every year, so text adds to context rather than replacing it.
